planting.note: Root short segments of the pencil-thin, club-tipped stems after a brief callusing period in a loose, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this Brazilian forest epiphyte branches in whorls that give mature clumps a distinctly segmented, jointed look.

directions: Grow in a chunky, humus-rich orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light to light shade, sheltering it from direct midday sun. Its slender cylindrical stem segments swell slightly toward each tip and branch in tight whorls of three or four, giving cascading clumps a beaded, club-like texture that sets it apart from the flatter-stemmed rhipsalis species already common in cultivation. Small cream to pale yellow flowers open along the stem tips in late winter, followed by translucent white berries. Water regularly enough to keep the mix from drying out fully, since this jungle epiphyte is far less drought-tolerant than desert cacti, and protect from frost as it is hardy outdoors only in the warmest zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root flattened stem-segment cuttings after callusing a few days in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this Brazilian rainforest endemic is uncommon in the wild but propagates readily from cuttings in cultivation.

directions: Pot in a coarse, well-drained, humus-rich mix and grow in bright indirect light to shade, avoiding direct sun that can scorch the thin, flattened stem segments. Each pad-like segment has a distinctive wavy, crimped margin that gives the plant a ruffled, papery texture quite different from the smooth-edged rhipsalis species already grown widely. Native to a narrow band of dry and moist forest in Brazil, it has become uncommon in the wild due to habitat loss even as it remains an easy, rewarding houseplant when propagated from cuttings. Keep the mix lightly and evenly moist rather than letting it dry out completely, and bring indoors well before frost since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in the mildest zones.
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

planting.note: Root cuttings of the ribbed, angled stem segments after callusing in a gritty, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this Brazilian epiphyte's faceted stems give it a more sculptural look than the round- or flat-stemmed rhipsalis species.

directions: Grow in a gritty, well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright indirect light to light shade, protecting the stems from harsh direct sun. Unlike the flat or cylindrical stems of most cultivated rhipsalis, this species produces stiffly ribbed, five-angled segments that give arching, cascading growth a distinctly faceted, sculptural profile. Small pale flowers form along the stem ridges, followed by translucent berries typical of the genus. Water moderately, letting the surface dry slightly between soakings, and move indoors or into a greenhouse ahead of cold weather, since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in frost-free climates.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root callused stem-segment cuttings in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; this Guatemalan cloud-forest epiphyte prefers the same humid, filtered-light conditions as its cultivated hybrid relatives.

directions: Plant in a chunky, well-drained orchid-bark or cactus mix and grow in bright indirect light, keeping the flattened, leaf-like stems out of direct midday sun. Native to cloud forests in Guatemala, this epiphytic species produces tubular, pink to magenta flowers that stand out against its arching, notch-edged stem segments. Water thoroughly during active growth, letting the mix dry somewhat between soakings, and mist occasionally to mimic the humid forest air of its native range. Move to a frost-free spot well ahead of cold weather, since it survives outdoors year-round only in the mildest, nearly frost-free zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem-segment cuttings after callusing in a fast-draining orchid-bark cactus mix in bright light with some direct morning sun; this Mexican and Central American species tolerates more sun than most jungle cacti, hence its common name.

directions: Grow in a fast-draining, chunky orchid-bark or cactus mix in bright light, allowing more direct sun than most jungle cacti tolerate since this species handles brighter exposure well, which is the source of its common name. Ranging naturally through Mexico, Honduras, and Guatemala, it produces vivid scarlet, funnel-shaped flowers on semi-climbing, segmented stems and has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit as a garden performer. Water regularly during the growing season, tapering off in cooler months, and provide sturdy support or a trellis for the sprawling, semi-climbing growth habit. Bring indoors or into a greenhouse before frost, since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in the warmest zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after callusing in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; as the type species of the genus Disocactus, this Guatemalan and Honduran epiphyte shows the classic shift from round to flattened stem growth.

directions: Plant in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark mix and grow in bright indirect light, shading from harsh direct sun. As the type species that gives the genus Disocactus its name, this Guatemalan and Honduran epiphyte has an unusual two-part growth habit, with new stems emerging round and pencil-like near the base before flattening into broader, leaf-like segments further out, giving the plant its common name. Water regularly enough to keep the mix from drying out completely during active growth, letting it dry slightly between soakings in cooler months. Protect from frost and move indoors well ahead of cold weather, since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in frost-free climates.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root a mature stem section after callusing in a chunky, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this Mexican cloud-forest species is CITES-listed and slow to establish, so start with a sizable cutting rather than a small tip.

directions: Grow in a chunky, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light, shielding the plant from direct midday sun. Its deeply divided, pinnately lobed stems resemble fern fronds far more than typical cactus growth, a trait unique among cultivated epiphyllums and the source of both its common names. Large, fragrant, white flowers with golden-yellow filaments open only at night, sometimes reaching over a foot long, on plants native to cloud forests in the Mexican states of Chiapas and Tabasco, where habitat loss has placed the species under CITES Appendix II protection. Water regularly during the growing season while allowing the mix to dry slightly between soakings, and bring indoors or into a greenhouse well before frost, since it survives outdoors year-round only in the mildest, essentially frost-free zones.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after callusing in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; as the type species of the genus, this wide-ranging tropical American epiphyte often roots into leaf litter that collects in tree hollows and cavities in the wild.

directions: Grow in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light to light shade, keeping the long, narrow, leaf-like stems out of direct sun. As the type species for the entire genus Epiphyllum, it is native across tropical forests from Central America into South America, where it commonly roots in leaf debris that accumulates in tree cavities rather than on open bark. Its slender, fragrant, night-opening flowers attract moth pollinators and are typically smaller and narrower than those of the large-flowered hybrid epiphyllums bred from it and its relatives. Water regularly enough to keep the mix from drying out fully, mist to raise humidity indoors, and protect from frost, since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in essentially frost-free climates.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after callusing in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this wide-ranging Central American and Caribbean epiphyte has also naturalized in Florida, where it climbs trees in frost-free hammocks.

directions: Plant in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark mix and grow in bright indirect light to light shade, protecting the long, climbing stems from harsh direct sun. Native from Mexico through Central America to Venezuela, this vining epiphyte has also naturalized in Florida and parts of the West Indies, scrambling up tree trunks in frost-free hammocks. Its showy white flowers characteristically open in twin pairs along the stem, a distinctive habit compared to the solitary blooms of many related species. Water regularly enough to keep the mix from drying out completely during active growth, and bring indoors or into a greenhouse well before frost, since it thrives outdoors year-round only in essentially frost-free zones.

planting.note: Root small stem segments after callusing in a well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright indirect light; this Brazilian mountain-forest species is a historic parent of the classic Christmas cactus and needs the same cool, dark fall period to set buds.

directions: Grow in a well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright indirect light to shade, letting the top of the mix dry slightly between waterings. Endemic to a small area of the Organ Mountains in southeastern Brazil, where it grows epiphytically in humid forest at high elevation, this species bears small, radially symmetrical pink flowers on tiny, notch-edged stem segments distinctly smaller than those of the truncata-derived cultivars that dominate the holiday-cactus trade. It is historically significant as one of the original parent species crossed to create the Buckleyi Group hybrids sold as classic Christmas cactus, and habitat loss has left the wild species listed as endangered. Provide roughly six weeks of cool nights and uninterrupted darkness in early fall to encourage a reliable bloom, and protect from frost since it is hardy outdoors only in essentially frost-free zones.
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

planting.note: Root stem-segment cuttings after callusing in a well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright indirect light; this Brazilian coastal-mountain species is the principal parent of the pastel-toned Reginae Group hybrid cultivars known among growers as 'The Queens'.

directions: Plant in a well-drained, humus-rich mix and grow in bright indirect light to shade, avoiding harsh direct sun on the broad, deeply toothed stem segments. Native to moist coastal mountain forests of southeastern Brazil, it produces unusually large flowers for the genus, shading from white at the center to rose-red at the petal tips, and can rebloom up to three times a year under good conditions. It is the key parent behind the Reginae Group of hybrid cultivars, colloquially called 'The Queens' among Schlumbergera growers for their oversized, richly shaded blooms. Provide the usual six weeks of cool nights and unbroken darkness in early fall to set buds reliably, and protect from frost, since it is hardy outdoors only in essentially frost-free zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Bristol Queen Christmas Cactus (Rose-Pink Reginae Group Holiday Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Bristol Queen belongs to the Reginae Group bred from Schlumbergera orssichiana and needs the standard fall regime of cool nights and long darkness to set buds.

directions: Pot in a well-drained, humus-rich mix and place in bright indirect light, letting the top inch dry between waterings. Bristol Queen belongs to the Reginae Group of Schlumbergera hybrids bred from Schlumbergera orssichiana, and its flowers show the broader form and shaded rose-pink coloring typical of that line, larger and softer in tone than the solid-color blooms of most truncata-derived cultivars. The flattened, scallop-edged stem segments branch into a dense, arching mound well suited to a hanging pot. Like its relatives, it needs roughly six weeks of cool nights and unbroken darkness in early fall to reliably set a full crop of winter flower buds.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
